title: Fashion Business Management: Running a Profitable Tailoring Business
subtitle: Cost and price your garments properly, manage orders, money and helpers, and sell confidently on WhatsApp and Instagram.
description: A practical course for tailors and fashion designers in Nigeria who want to run their business professionally. You will define your customer, cost a garment line by line and price it for profit, run every order through a clear workflow with deposits and an order book, keep a simple cash book, control quality, manage apprentices fairly, measure monthly performance and build a WhatsApp Business catalogue that sells.
outcomes: Cost any garment from fabric, lining, trims, labour and overheads, and set a price for a target margin
Run orders through a six-stage workflow with an order book, written terms, deposits and fittings
Keep a daily cash book, track balances owed and work out monthly profit
Apply a pre-delivery quality checklist and plan busy seasons within real capacity
Manage apprentices and helpers with written agreements, fair pay and safe practice
Build a WhatsApp Business catalogue and sales toolkit, take payments safely and write a 90-day growth plan
audience: Women who already sew or run a small tailoring or fashion business and want to price correctly, stay organised and grow into a recognised brand.
tools: Smartphone with WhatsApp Business (and optionally Instagram and Google Sheets)
Notebook for an order book and cash book, and a receipt book
Tape measure, your usual sewing tools and recent receipts for materials
Access to the CAC online portal if you are registering a business name

modules.title: Foundations: Your Fashion Business, Its Language and Its Setup
modules.overview: Decide what kind of fashion business you are running and who it serves, learn the money words every tailor needs, and set up your workshop, registration and safety rules properly before taking more orders.

lessons.title: Choosing your business model and your customer
objectives: Describe the main fashion business models in Nigeria: bespoke, group orders, ready-to-wear, alterations and uniforms
Compare bespoke tailoring with ready-to-wear on cash flow, risk and workload
Define one clear customer group and the season when she buys
Write a one-sentence description of what your business sells and to whom

blocks.text: Many talented tailors stay small for years, not because their sewing is poor, but because they run the business like a hobby. They accept every style, quote prices from their head, mix shop money with house money and sew late into the night before every festive season. This course is about the **business side** of fashion: what you sell, how you cost and price it, how you manage orders, money and people, and how you sell online. You already know how to sew, or you work with someone who does. Now you will learn to run it professionally.

blocks.name: trying-on-clothes
blocks.alt: A woman trying on a garment in front of a mirror
blocks.caption: Every fashion business starts with a clear picture of the woman who will wear the clothes and pay for them.

blocks.text: Five ways to earn from fashion

head: Model
What you sell
How money comes in
Main risk
rows: One garment sewn for one client's measurements
Deposit before cutting, balance at collection
Many outfits for one wedding, burial or church event
Large deposits close to the event date
Many deadlines on the same day
Finished pieces in standard sizes, sold from stock
Money tied up in unsold stock
Small cash payments, often same day
School, church, staff or hotel uniforms in bulk
Waiting a long time to be paid

blocks.text: Most Nigerian tailors start with **bespoke** work: the client brings fabric, you take measurements, she pays a deposit and collects later. Bespoke work needs little stock, because the client usually supplies the fabric, but your income depends on your hours. **Ready-to-wear** can grow beyond your own hands because you can sew in batches, but you must buy fabric first and wait for buyers. Many successful small brands mix the two: bespoke work pays the bills while a small RTW line builds the brand.

blocks.title: Bespoke vs ready-to-wear
items: Bespoke
Ready-to-wear
blocks.caption: Bespoke is safer for cash flow; ready-to-wear can grow further but ties up money in stock.

blocks.text: Know your customer, not just your style

Saying 'I sew for everybody' feels safe but makes marketing hard. A **customer group** (also called a niche) is a group of people with the same need, budget and buying habits. Examples: working women who need corporate gowns and skirt suits; brides and their families buying aso-ebi; men who wear senator and kaftan styles to church and events; mothers buying children's party wear; plus-size women who struggle to find good fits in ready-made clothes.

items: **Who is she?** Age range, work, where she lives, how she dresses on a normal day.
**What does she buy?** Styles, fabrics (Ankara, lace, aso-oke, adire, plain cotton), how often.
**What does she spend?** A realistic price band per outfit in your area.
**When does she buy?** Christmas and New Year, Easter, Eid (Sallah), wedding seasons, school resumption, end-of-year office parties.
**Where does she look?** WhatsApp status, Instagram, church or mosque groups, word of mouth, a market shop.

blocks.title: Plan for your peak season
blocks.text: Festive periods bring more orders than one person can sew. Decide in advance the date after which you stop accepting orders for that season, and tell clients early. A clear cut-off protects your name better than rushed, late outfits.

blocks.title: Worked example: narrowing the business
blocks.context: For example, Chiamaka runs a two-machine shop in Owerri. She sews anything that walks in: school uniforms, men's trousers, bridal gowns and repairs. She is always busy but rarely has savings.
steps: She looks back over her last 40 orders in her notebook and groups them: 22 women's gowns and skirt suits, 8 men's styles, 6 repairs, 4 bridal pieces.
She notes that the women's office wear came mostly from referrals among bank and school staff, and that these clients paid deposits without long bargaining.
She notes that bridal pieces took about three times longer than a gown and caused the most fitting disputes.
She writes her statement: 'I make well-fitted office and church wear for working women in Owerri, ready in 7 to 10 days.'
She keeps repairs as a small side service but stops accepting bridal gowns until she has trained help.
blocks.result: Chiamaka now has a clear customer to market to, a turnaround time she can promise, and fewer jobs that eat her time. Her marketing can speak directly to working women instead of everybody.

blocks.text: Your one-sentence business statement

Write one sentence using this pattern: **I make [what] for [whom] in [where], [your promise].** The promise should be something you can keep every time, such as a turnaround time, a fit guarantee with one free adjustment, or a finish quality. You will use this sentence in your WhatsApp Business profile, your Instagram bio and when people ask what you do.

Your statement also guides your prices. If you promise fine finishing for working women, you cannot price like a roadside repair stall, and you should not try to. Look at three or four tailors who serve the same customer in your area, note roughly what they charge and how fast they deliver, and decide whether you will compete on speed, finish, fit or style. Choose one main strength and make sure your work shows it every time.

takeaways: Bespoke, group orders, ready-to-wear, alterations and uniforms carry different cash and risk patterns
Bespoke protects cash flow; ready-to-wear can grow but ties money in stock
A clear customer group makes pricing and marketing easier
Plan for peak seasons with a firm order cut-off date

activity.title: Review your last orders and define your customer
steps: List your last 20 to 40 orders from memory, your notebook or WhatsApp chats.
Group them by type (women's gowns, men's styles, repairs, bridal, uniforms).
Mark which groups paid on time and which caused the most stress or disputes.
Answer the five customer questions for the group you want to focus on.
Write your one-sentence business statement.
activity.evidence: A photo of your grouped order list, your five customer answers and your business statement.

lessons.title: The money words every tailor must know
objectives: Explain direct costs, labour, overheads, price and profit in plain words
Calculate profit margin and markup from cost and selling price
Use the terms deposit, balance, turnaround time and order book correctly
Spot the difference between sales (money in) and profit (money kept)

blocks.text: When a client asks 'How much?', many tailors answer with whatever the shop next door charges. That price may not cover your own costs. To price well you need a small set of words, and the habit of using them every time. This lesson gives you that vocabulary with numbers you can follow on a calculator.

blocks.name: calculator
blocks.alt: A person working figures on a large calculator
blocks.caption: Pricing is not guessing: a few simple calculations tell you whether an order is worth taking.

blocks.text: The cost words

head: Term
Plain meaning
Tailoring example
rows: Everything that goes into this one garment
Fabric, lining, interfacing, zip, buttons, thread, hooks
The value of the time spent making it
Cutting, sewing, finishing, fitting hours, yours or an employee's
Running costs that are not tied to one garment
Shop rent, fuel and electricity, data, needles, machine servicing, transport to market
Materials plus labour plus share of overheads
What this garment really costs you before profit
The amount on your price list or quote
What the business keeps from this order

blocks.text: The most forgotten cost is **your own labour**. If you do not pay yourself for your hours inside the price, you are working for free and calling the leftover money 'profit'. The second most forgotten cost is **overheads**. Fuel for the generator, shop rent and data are real costs of every garment, even though they are paid monthly.
Putting a value on your hour

To include labour, you need an **hourly labour rate**. A simple way: decide what you want to earn as a wage in a normal month, then divide it by the hours you actually sew in that month. For example, if you want about 150,000 naira (approximate) as your own wage and you sew about 150 hours a month (6 hours a day for 25 days), your rate is 150,000 / 150 = 1,000 naira per hour. A gown that takes 8 hours then carries 8,000 naira of labour. If you pay a helper, use what you actually pay her per hour for the work she does. Count only real sewing hours: time spent waiting for light, going to market or chatting with clients belongs in overheads, not in labour.
Margin and markup: two ways to describe profit

**Markup** compares profit with cost. **Margin** compares profit with selling price. They use the same profit but give different percentages, and mixing them up is a common reason tailors undercharge.

blocks.title: Worked example: margin and markup on one gown
blocks.context: For example, Bisi's total cost for a lined Ankara gown is about 30,000 naira (approximate). She sells it for 40,000 naira.
steps: Profit = selling price minus total cost = 40,000 minus 30,000 = 10,000 naira.
Markup = profit divided by cost = 10,000 / 30,000 = 0.333, so about 33%.
Margin = profit divided by selling price = 10,000 / 40,000 = 0.25, so 25%.
If Bisi wants a 25% margin on a garment costing 30,000, she divides cost by (1 minus 0.25): 30,000 / 0.75 = 40,000.
If she wrongly adds 25% to cost (30,000 x 1.25 = 37,500), her margin is only 7,500 / 37,500 = 20%.
blocks.result: The same 10,000 naira profit is a 33% markup but a 25% margin. To hit a target margin, divide cost by (1 minus the margin), do not just add the percentage to cost.

blocks.title: What a price is built from
items: Profit
Overhead share
Labour
Direct materials
blocks.caption: Materials are the base; labour and overheads sit on top, and profit is only what remains above all three.

blocks.text: The order words

items: **Deposit:** part payment made before you start, usually enough to cover at least the materials you must buy.
**Balance:** the rest of the price, paid at collection or before delivery.
**Turnaround time:** the number of days from measurement and deposit to a ready garment.
**Order book:** your record of every order: client, style, measurements, price, deposit, balance, due date and status.
**Fitting:** the try-on before final finishing, where you adjust for fit.
**Alteration window:** the period after collection when you will adjust fit at no extra charge.

blocks.text: Sales are not profit

If you collect 500,000 naira from clients in December, that is your **sales** (also called revenue or turnover). It is not your income. Out of it you paid for fabric and lining, paid helpers, bought fuel and paid rent. What remains after all costs is your **profit**. A busy month with poor pricing can bring large sales and very little profit. You will learn to record both in Module 2.

blocks.title: Deposits are not yet yours
blocks.text: A deposit for an order you have not finished is money you still owe in work. If you spend all December deposits on house needs and then cannot buy lining or pay for fuel, the orders fail. Keep deposits for the orders they were paid for until those orders are delivered.

takeaways: Total cost = direct materials + labour + share of overheads
Pay yourself for your hours inside the price, or you are working for free
Markup compares profit with cost; margin compares profit with price
To reach a target margin, divide cost by (1 minus margin)
Sales are money in; profit is what is left after every cost

activity.title: Calculate margin and markup on your own work
steps: Choose one garment you sewed recently and write down its selling price.
List every material you used and its approximate cost.
Estimate the hours you spent and give each hour a value you think is fair.
Add a rough overhead amount, then calculate total cost, profit, markup and margin.
Write one sentence: was the price high enough?
activity.evidence: A photo of your handwritten calculation showing cost, price, profit, markup and margin.

lessons.title: Setting up properly: workspace, CAC registration and safety
objectives: Organise a workspace with the tools a professional tailoring business needs
Outline the steps to register a business name with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC)
Apply electrical, fire, generator and tool safety rules in the workshop
Protect clients' measurements, photos and phone numbers as personal data

blocks.text: A professional setup does not need a big shop. It needs the right tools in the right place, a legal identity that lets you open a business account and bid for larger jobs, and safety rules that protect you, your helpers and your clients' clothes. This lesson covers all three.

blocks.name: sewing-needle
blocks.caption: Good tools, kept in order and kept safe, are the base of a professional workshop.

blocks.text: Workshop tools and organisation

items: **Machines:** a straight-stitch machine (manual or electric), and ideally an overlock (serger) for clean seam finishes.
**Cutting:** sharp fabric scissors used only on fabric, pinking shears, a seam ripper, tailor's chalk and a cutting table.
**Measuring:** a good tape measure (replace it when it stretches), a metre rule and a hip curve or French curve if you draft patterns.
**Pressing:** an iron and ironing board; pressing during sewing makes a big difference to the finish.
**Storage:** labelled bags or shelves for each client's fabric with her name, order number and due date.
**Records:** an order book or notebook, a receipt book, and a phone with WhatsApp Business.

blocks.title: Label every client's fabric
blocks.text: Lost or mixed-up fabric is one of the most painful disputes in tailoring. The moment a client hands over fabric, tag it with her name, phone number, order number and due date, and photograph it with the tag. That photo is your proof if anything is questioned later.
Registering a business name with CAC

In Nigeria, a business name (for example 'Ada Stitches') is registered with the **Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC)** through its online portal. A registered business name lets you open a business bank account in that name, issue proper receipts, and apply for uniform contracts or programmes that ask for registration. It is different from a limited company: a business name does not have a separate legal personality, so the owner remains personally responsible for its debts.

items: Choose two or more possible names and search for them on the CAC portal; an approved name is reserved for a limited time while you complete registration.
Fill the business name registration form online with the business address, the nature of the business (for example tailoring and fashion design) and the details of each proprietor.
Upload what the portal asks for, such as a means of identification, passport photograph and signature.
Pay the filing fee on the portal (check the current fee on the CAC website or portal at the time).
When approved, download your certificate from your CAC dashboard.
Each year, file the business name's annual return with CAC; late filing attracts penalties.

blocks.title: Avoid registration scams
blocks.text: Use the official CAC website and portal, or an accredited agent you can verify. Do not pay a stranger on social media who promises a certificate 'in one hour'. Keep copies of every payment receipt and your login details private.
Workshop safety

items: **Electricity:** do not overload one extension socket with the iron, machines and phone chargers; the iron alone draws a lot of power. Use a voltage stabiliser or surge protector for electric machines, and switch off and unplug everything at closing time.
**Generator:** never run a generator indoors, in a passage or near windows. Its exhaust contains carbon monoxide, a gas you cannot see or smell, which can kill.
**Fire:** keep fabric, paper patterns and fuel away from the iron and any heat source. Keep a fire extinguisher or a bucket of sand where you can reach it and know how to use it.
**Needles and blades:** keep fingers clear of the needle, change bent needles at once, store pins in a cushion and keep scissors closed when not in use.
**Body:** work in good light, take short breaks to stretch your back, neck and eyes, and keep the floor clear of offcuts to prevent falls.

blocks.text: Clients' data is personal data

Measurements, phone numbers, addresses and photos of clients are personal information. Nigeria's **Data Protection Act 2023** sets rules for how businesses handle personal data. In practice: keep your order book where others cannot read it, do not share a client's measurements or number with anyone else, and ask permission before posting a photo of a client wearing your work.

blocks.title: Worked example: a one-week setup plan
blocks.context: For example, Halima sews from a room in her house in Kaduna and wants to look and work more professionally before the next festive season.
steps: Day 1: she sorts all client fabric into labelled bags and photographs each one with its tag.
Day 2: she replaces her stretched tape measure and frees one extension socket for the iron alone.
Day 3: she moves the generator outside, away from the window, and buys a small fire extinguisher.
Day 4: she searches two business names on the CAC portal and starts the registration form.
Day 5: she starts a new order book and sets up WhatsApp Business with her business statement.
blocks.result: In five days Halima reduces her risk of lost fabric, electrical fire and generator fumes, and starts her legal registration, all without renting a shop.

blocks.title: Ready-to-trade checklist
items: Fabric tagged and photographed
Iron on its own socket
Generator outside, extinguisher ready
CAC business name started
Order book and receipts ready
Client data kept private
blocks.caption: Tick each item before taking your next big batch of orders.

takeaways: Tag and photograph every client's fabric the moment you receive it
A CAC business name enables a business account and contracts, but the owner stays personally liable
File the business name annual return with CAC each year
Never run a generator indoors; do not overload sockets with the iron
Treat measurements, numbers and photos as private client data

activity.title: Run a workshop safety and setup audit
steps: Walk through your workspace with the ready-to-trade checklist.
Photograph any risk you find (overloaded socket, generator position, untagged fabric).
Fix at least two risks this week and photograph the fixed version.
Search two possible business names on the CAC portal and note the result.
activity.evidence: Before-and-after photos of two fixes and a note of the business names you searched.

quiz.q: Ifeoma sews only bespoke gowns with fabric clients bring. Compared with starting a ready-to-wear line, what is the main advantage for her cash flow?
options: She is paid deposits before work and does not tie money up in stock
She never has to deal with fitting problems
She can sew unlimited orders without extra hands
She does not need to keep any records
quiz.explain: Bespoke work usually starts with a deposit and the client often supplies fabric, so little money is tied up in stock. Fitting issues and capacity limits still exist.

quiz.q: A skirt suit costs 24,000 naira in total. Kemi wants a 20% margin. What price should she charge?
quiz.explain: Price = cost / (1 minus margin) = 24,000 / 0.8 = 30,000. Adding 20% to cost (28,800) gives a margin of only about 16.7%.

quiz.q: Which of these is an overhead rather than a direct material?
quiz.explain: Fuel is a running cost shared across all garments, so it is an overhead. Lining, zips and buttons go into one specific garment.

quiz.q: Ngozi collected 600,000 naira in December. What can she correctly say about her profit?
options: Her profit is 600,000 minus all her costs for those orders
Her profit is the deposits only
Profit cannot be known without CAC registration
quiz.explain: 600,000 is sales. Profit is what remains after materials, labour, overheads and other costs are taken out.

quiz.q: Amaka is registering 'Amaka Couture' as a business name with CAC. Which statement is true?
options: It makes the business a separate legal person, so she has no personal liability
It never needs any filing again after registration
It must file an annual return, and she remains personally liable for its debts
It can only be done in person at a CAC office
quiz.explain: A business name has no separate legal personality, so the owner is personally liable. Business names file annual returns, and registration is done through the CAC online portal.

quiz.q: Where should a tailor run her generator?
options: Outside, away from doors and windows
In the shop passage so it is safe from thieves
Inside the shop with the window open
Under the cutting table to save space
quiz.explain: Generator exhaust contains carbon monoxide, which can kill. It must run outdoors, away from openings into the building.

modules.title: Guided Practice: Orders, Costing and Money Records
modules.overview: Run every order through the same clear steps, cost a real garment line by line and turn that cost into a price, then keep simple records of deposits, balances, income and spending so you always know where the money is.

lessons.title: From consultation to collection: the order workflow and order book
objectives: Follow a six-stage order workflow from consultation to collection
Record a complete order in an order book with measurements, price, deposit and due date
Set realistic due dates using your weekly sewing capacity
Agree clear order terms with a client before cutting

blocks.text: Late outfits, lost measurements and arguments over balances usually come from the same root: no fixed process. When every order goes through the same stages, and every stage leaves a written record, you can take more orders with less stress. This lesson gives you that process and the order book that holds it together.

blocks.name: order-confirmed
blocks.alt: A person confirming an order on a large screen
blocks.caption: A confirmed order means agreed style, price, deposit and date, written down, not just discussed.

blocks.title: The bespoke order workflow
items: Consult and agree style
Measure and record
Deposit and receipt
Cut and sew
Fitting and adjust
Finish, collect, balance
blocks.caption: Each stage ends with something written or photographed, so nothing depends on memory.

blocks.text: Stage by stage

items: **Consult.** Look at the style picture with the client, agree details (neckline, sleeve, length, lining, closures) and check that her fabric is enough. Write the style details and save the picture in her WhatsApp chat.

**Measure.** Take measurements with a good tape over light clothing and record them on her order page. For a women's gown this usually includes bust, under-bust, waist, hip, shoulder, bust point, half length (shoulder to waist), full length, sleeve length and round sleeve or arm.
**Deposit.** Agree the price and take a deposit that covers at least the materials you must buy. Issue a receipt with the order number, amount paid and balance.
**Cut and sew.** Schedule the order into a specific week. Pre-wash cotton fabrics such as some Ankara if the client agrees, because untreated cotton can shrink after the first wash.
**Fitting.** Invite the client for a try-on before final finishing. Note every adjustment on her page and agree a new date if needed.
**Finish and collect.** Press, check against your quality checklist, photograph the finished piece, collect the balance and only then release the garment.

blocks.text: Measurements are the part most likely to go wrong. Measure in the same order every time so you never skip one, keep the tape snug but not tight, and read it at eye level. Write the date beside every set, because bodies change: re-measure a returning client if it has been several months or she tells you her size has changed. If an apprentice takes measurements, check two or three of them yourself before cutting.
What goes in the order book

head: Field
Example entry
rows: Ada (number kept private in the book)
Fitted gown, flared sleeve, 6 yards Ankara (client's), lined
Measured, Cutting, Sewing, Fitting, Ready, Collected

blocks.text: A paper notebook works well if you use one page per order and write the order number on the client's fabric tag. Some tailors also keep a simple spreadsheet in Google Sheets on the phone, with one row per order and a status column. Whatever you use, update the status the same day it changes.
Setting due dates you can keep

Your **capacity** is how many garments you can finish in a week. Count real sewing hours, not hours in the shop. If you sew about 30 hours a week and an average gown takes about 8 hours, your capacity is about 3 to 4 gowns a week. Before you promise a date, look at what is already booked in that week.

blocks.title: Worked example: can she accept this order?
blocks.context: For example, Funmi sews about 30 hours a week in her Ibadan shop. A client asks on Monday for a lined gown by Saturday of next week.
steps: Funmi checks her order book: this week has 3 gowns (about 24 hours) and next week has 2 gowns and a skirt suit (about 16 plus 10 hours).
This week is nearly full (24 of 30 hours). Next week has 26 of 30 hours booked, leaving about 4 hours.
The new gown needs about 8 hours, plus a fitting. It does not fit next week without overtime.
She offers two options: delivery in two weeks at the normal price, or next Saturday with an express charge that covers paid help from a trained helper.
The client chooses the two-week date. Funmi writes it in the book with a fitting date.
blocks.result: By checking capacity before saying yes, Funmi avoids a late delivery and offers an honest choice. The express option is priced to pay for the extra hands it needs.

blocks.text: Agree your terms in writing

items: The deposit amount and that cutting starts only after it is paid.
The due date, and that changes to the style after cutting may change the price and date.
How long you will keep an uncollected garment, and that balance is paid before collection.
Your alteration window, for example one free adjustment within 7 days of collection.
That the client should check her fabric quantity; shortfalls are her cost to buy.

blocks.title: Send terms on WhatsApp
blocks.text: Save your terms as a Quick Reply in WhatsApp Business and send them with every new order. When a client replies 'OK', you have a written record of what was agreed.

takeaways: Use the same six stages for every order and leave a record at each stage
One order page with measurements, price, deposit, balance and dates prevents most disputes
Promise dates from your weekly capacity, not from hope
Send written terms before cutting and keep the client's agreement

activity.title: Set up your order book
steps: Create an order page template (paper or Google Sheets) with all the fields in this lesson.
Enter your current open orders, including deposits paid and balances due.
Calculate your weekly capacity in sewing hours and garments.
Write your order terms and save them as a WhatsApp Quick Reply.
activity.evidence: A photo or screenshot of your order book with at least three complete entries, and your saved terms.

lessons.title: Costing a garment and setting a profitable price
objectives: Cost a lined garment line by line: fabric, lining, trims, labour and overheads
Calculate an overhead rate per sewing hour from monthly running costs
Price both a full package (you supply fabric) and a sewing fee (client supplies fabric)
Decide when a price is too low to accept

blocks.text: In Nigeria, two kinds of price are common. With a **sewing fee** (also called workmanship), the client brings her fabric and you charge for making it. With a **full package**, you supply the fabric and everything else. You need to cost both correctly. The method is the same: add materials, labour and overheads, then add profit using the margin method from Module 1.

blocks.name: spool-of-thread
blocks.caption: Even small items like thread, zips and interfacing belong in the cost of every garment.

blocks.text: Step 1: Find your overhead rate
List your monthly running costs and divide by the sewing hours you work in a month. This gives an **overhead rate per hour** that you add to every garment according to how long it takes.

If you sew about 200 hours a month (8 hours a day for 25 days), the overhead rate is 100,000 / 200 = **500 naira per hour**. If you sew fewer hours, the rate goes up, because the same rent and fuel are shared across fewer garments.
Step 2: Cost the garment

blocks.title: Worked example: full-package lined Ankara gown
blocks.context: For example, Zainab in Abuja makes a fitted, lined Ankara gown and supplies all materials. Prices below are approximate and vary by market and quality.
steps: Fabric: one 6-yard piece of Ankara at about 15,000 naira.
Lining: 3 yards at about 1,000 naira per yard = 3,000 naira.
Trims: interfacing, invisible zip, thread and hooks = about 2,000 naira. Direct materials total = 20,000 naira.
Labour: 1 hour cutting, 5 hours sewing, 1 hour finishing and pressing, 1 hour for fitting = 8 hours x 1,000 naira = 8,000 naira.
Overheads: 8 hours x 500 naira = 4,000 naira.
Price for a 25% margin = 32,000 / 0.75 = 42,667 naira, rounded to 43,000 naira.
blocks.result: Zainab's full-package price is about 43,000 naira, giving roughly 11,000 naira profit on top of paying herself 8,000 naira for her labour. Anything below 32,000 naira loses money.

blocks.title: Worked example: the same gown as a sewing fee
blocks.context: For example, the next client brings her own Ankara and lining. Zainab supplies only the trims.
steps: Trims: 2,000 naira.
Labour: 8,000 naira. Overheads: 4,000 naira.
Total cost = 14,000 naira.
Price for a 25% margin = 14,000 / 0.75 = 18,667, rounded to 19,000 naira.
blocks.result: Her sewing fee for this style is about 19,000 naira. If the shop next door charges 12,000 naira, Zainab now knows she cannot match that without losing money, so she competes on fit and finish instead.

blocks.title: From cost to price
items: List materials
Add labour hours
Add overhead per hour
Total cost
Divide by (1 minus margin)
Round and quote
blocks.caption: The same six steps work for any garment, from a simple skirt to an aso-ebi order.

blocks.text: Step 3: Check your price against the market

After costing, compare your price with three or four tailors who serve the same customer. If your price is much higher, look for waste before you cut your margin: are you buying lining in small pieces at a high price instead of by the roll? Are you losing hours to rework because of measuring mistakes? Is your overhead rate high because you sew few hours while paying for a large shop? If your price is much lower than theirs, you may be undercharging for good work, and you can raise it gradually as your portfolio grows.

When a client asks you to reduce your price, change the order rather than your margin. Offer a simpler style, no lining, fewer embellishments or a longer turnaround. That way the price comes down because the cost came down, and you still earn on every garment.
Pricing decisions that protect you

items: **Group orders:** cost one outfit, then check whether bulk fabric buying lowers material cost. Do not discount labour unless the styles are identical and faster to repeat.
**Express orders:** add a charge that pays for overtime or a helper.
**Complex styles:** heavy beading, corsets and stone work can take several times longer than a plain gown. Time yourself once and cost from real hours.

**Rising fabric prices:** fabric prices change often, so date your price list and review it regularly. For full-package orders, quote fabric at today's price and buy it as soon as the deposit arrives.
**Floor price:** your total cost is the lowest price you can accept. Below that, every order makes you poorer.

blocks.title: Watch a pricing walkthrough
blocks.text: The video below discusses how a tailor can work out what to charge for sewing services. Compare the method with the cost-plus-margin steps here, and use your own Nigerian costs and hours.

takeaways: Overhead rate = monthly running costs / monthly sewing hours
Total cost = materials + (hours x labour rate) + (hours x overhead rate)
Price = total cost / (1 minus target margin), then round
Your total cost is your floor price; never quote below it
Date your price list and review it as fabric prices change

activity.title: Build a costing sheet for your best-selling style
steps: List your real monthly overheads and calculate your overhead rate per sewing hour.
Time yourself making your most common style, or estimate carefully from your last one.
Cost it as a full package and as a sewing fee using the steps in this lesson.
Compare both prices with what you charge today and note the difference.
Decide your new price and the date you will start using it.
activity.evidence: A completed costing sheet (paper or spreadsheet) for one style showing overhead rate, total cost and both prices.

lessons.title: Deposits, cash flow and simple bookkeeping
objectives: Keep a daily cash book that records money in and money out
Separate business money from household money using a business account
Track deposits and balances so no payment is forgotten
Work out monthly profit from your records

blocks.text: Bookkeeping simply means writing down every naira that comes in or goes out of the business, the same day. It does not need accounting training. It answers three questions every owner should be able to answer at any time: How much money does the business have? Who still owes me? Did I make a profit last month?

blocks.name: ledger
blocks.caption: A simple cash book, filled in daily, is the most useful financial tool a small fashion business can have.

blocks.text: Separate the money first

Open a separate account for the business: a business account in your registered business name, or at least a separate personal account used only for the shop. Ask clients to pay deposits and balances into it by transfer or POS. Pay yourself a fixed amount from it each week or month as your wage, and move it to your personal account. This one habit makes bookkeeping far easier, because your bank statement becomes a second record of business money.
Choosing your deposit level

Set your deposit so that, if a client disappears, you have not lost money. For full-package orders, the deposit should at least cover the fabric, lining and trims you will buy, because you cannot resell fabric cut to one person's size. For sewing-fee orders where the client brings fabric, many tailors ask for half or more before cutting. For large group orders, such as aso-ebi for a wedding, ask for deposits on every outfit before buying in bulk, and set a firm last date for measurements so you have time to sew. Write your deposit rule into your terms and apply it to everyone, including friends and church members.
The daily cash book

Write each entry the same day. Note the order number for every deposit and balance, and how it was paid (cash, transfer, POS). At the end of each day, check that the cash in your drawer plus your business account matches the balance column. If it does not, find the difference before you forget what happened.
Paying yourself

Many owners take money from the drawer whenever there is a need at home. That makes it impossible to know whether the business is profitable. Instead, decide a fixed wage, for example a set amount every Friday, and record it in the cash book as 'Owner's wage'. If the business has a good month, you can take an extra amount at month end once all bills and balances are settled. If a month is slow, the cash book shows it early, and you can cut costs or push sales before the money runs out.
Tracking who owes you

Keep a short **balances owed** list: order number, client, balance and due date. Review it every Monday. When a garment is ready, send a polite WhatsApp message with a photo and the balance due. A garment that sits uncollected is money already spent on materials and labour that has not come back.

blocks.title: The tailoring cash cycle
items: Deposit received
Materials bought
Garment sewn
Balance collected
Bills and wage paid
blocks.caption: Money goes round this cycle with every order; a break at any point, such as uncollected balances, starves the next order.

blocks.title: Worked example: working out March profit
blocks.context: For example, Esther in Port Harcourt totals her cash book at the end of March. All figures are approximate.
steps: Money in from orders (deposits and balances): 480,000 naira.
Materials bought for orders: 190,000 naira.
Helper's pay: 60,000 naira. Overheads (rent share, fuel, data, transport): 100,000 naira.
Total business costs = 190,000 + 60,000 + 100,000 = 350,000 naira.
Profit before her own wage = 480,000 minus 350,000 = 130,000 naira.
She also checks her balances owed list: 70,000 naira is still owed for finished garments.
blocks.result: Esther made about 130,000 naira for her own work and the business in March, and has 70,000 naira to collect. She now knows her real earnings instead of guessing from a busy shop.

blocks.title: Fake transfer alerts
blocks.text: Some fraudsters send fake SMS 'credit alerts' or edited screenshots and then rush to collect a garment. Before releasing any garment, confirm the money has arrived by checking your banking app or bank statement, not the SMS or a screenshot. Never share your PIN, password or one-time code (OTP) with anyone.

items: Keep all receipts for purchases in an envelope or photograph them into a phone folder for each month.
Give the client a receipt for every payment, showing amount paid and balance remaining.
Do your monthly total within the first week of the next month.
If you prefer an app, a spreadsheet in Google Sheets with the same five columns works well.

takeaways: Write every naira in and out the same day, with the order number
Use a separate business account and pay yourself a fixed wage
Review the balances owed list weekly and chase politely
Monthly profit = money in minus all business costs
Confirm transfers in your banking app, never from an SMS or screenshot

activity.title: Keep a cash book for two weeks
steps: Start a cash book with the five columns in this lesson and your opening balance.
Record every business payment in and out for 14 days, with order numbers.
Each evening, check that drawer cash plus account balance matches your book.
Make a balances owed list and send at least one polite collection message.
At the end, total money in and money out for the two weeks.
activity.evidence: Photos of two weeks of cash book pages, your balances owed list and your two-week totals.

quiz.q: A client asks for a gown in 5 days. Your order book shows that week already has 28 of your 30 sewing hours booked. The gown takes about 8 hours. What is the best response?
options: Accept and sew through the night
Offer a later date, or an express price that pays for extra help
Refuse to work with her ever
quiz.explain: Capacity is nearly full, so an honest later date or a priced express option protects quality and your reputation.

quiz.q: Your monthly overheads are 90,000 naira and you sew about 180 hours a month. What is your overhead rate per hour?
quiz.explain: 90,000 / 180 = 500 naira per sewing hour.

quiz.q: A shirt uses 9,000 naira of materials, takes 4 hours at a 1,000 naira labour rate, and your overhead rate is 500 naira per hour. What is the total cost?
Using that total cost of 15,000 naira, what price gives a 25% margin?
quiz.explain: 15,000 / 0.75 = 20,000 naira. Adding 25% to cost (18,750) would give only a 20% margin.

quiz.q: A client shows an SMS credit alert and asks to collect her outfit immediately. What should the tailor do first?
options: Release the outfit, an SMS is proof
Check the business banking app to confirm the money has arrived
quiz.explain: SMS alerts and screenshots can be faked. Confirm the credit in your banking app or statement before releasing the garment. Never ask for or share an OTP.

quiz.q: Why should deposits and balances be recorded with the order number?
options: It is required to open a bank account
So clients cannot ask for receipts
So you can see which orders are paid, which still owe, and match money to work
quiz.explain: Linking each payment to an order lets you track balances owed and see whether each order covered its costs.

modules.title: Quality, People and Measurement
modules.overview: Prevent the mistakes that cost tailors their clients, manage apprentices and helpers fairly and safely, and measure the few numbers that show whether the business is truly improving.

lessons.title: Quality control: fit, finish and on-time delivery
objectives: Identify the most common quality failures in tailoring and their causes
Use a pre-delivery quality checklist on every garment
Handle a fitting complaint calmly with a clear alteration policy
Plan a festive season so quality does not drop under pressure

blocks.text: In fashion, one badly fitted outfit at a wedding is seen by hundreds of guests, and the story travels faster than any advert. Quality is not only neat stitching. For your client it means three things: **it fits**, **it is well finished**, and **it is ready when promised**. This lesson shows how to protect all three with simple checks.

blocks.name: dress
blocks.caption: A finished garment should pass the same quality checks every time before it leaves the shop.

blocks.text: Common failures and how to prevent them

head: Problem
Usual cause
Prevention
rows: Wrong or old measurements, no ease allowed
Measure in a fixed order, date measurements, allow ease for movement, always do a fitting
Offer to pre-wash cotton fabrics such as some Ankara before cutting, with the client's agreement
Colour running onto lining or skin
Dye not fixed in the fabric
Test a small offcut in water first; warn the client and advise cold hand-washing if colour runs
Wrong thread tension, blunt or wrong needle, not pressing
Test stitch on an offcut, change needles often, press each seam as you sew
Overlock, zigzag or bind every raw edge
Mark hems on the body at fitting, plan motif placement before cutting
Too many orders accepted, no capacity check
Book orders against weekly capacity and set a season cut-off date

blocks.text: The pre-delivery checklist

blocks.title: Before any garment leaves
items: Measurements match order page
Seams finished and pressed
Hem level, threads trimmed
Zip and fastenings work smoothly
No marks, stains or chalk
Photo taken for records
blocks.caption: A two-minute check catches most problems before the client sees them.

blocks.text: Hang the garment, turn it inside out and look at every seam. Try every zip and hook. Measure key points (bust, waist, length) against the order page. Remove all chalk marks and loose threads, then press. Photograph it front and back. If an apprentice did the work, the owner or senior tailor does this check, not the person who sewed it.
Why the fitting matters so much

Skipping the fitting to save time is the most expensive shortcut in tailoring. At a fitting, the garment is sewn but not finished: side seams can still be taken in or let out, the hem is not yet sewn, and sleeves can be adjusted. After finishing, the same change means unpicking overlocked seams and pressed hems, which takes longer and can leave marks. Book the fitting when you take the deposit, so the client plans for it. If a client cannot come, ask her to send a well-fitting garment of her own, and compare its measurements with your work.

Also check fabric before you cut. Look for flaws, holes or printing faults along the whole length, and show the client any you find. Lay the pattern so motifs line up at the centre front and across seams where the style needs it, and confirm she has enough fabric for her chosen style before cutting the first piece.
Handling a fitting complaint

items: Listen fully and ask her to show you where it does not fit. Do not argue in front of others.
Ask her to try it on, and pin or chalk the problem area.
Check the order page: was the error in measuring, cutting or a change in her body or wish?
If it is your error, adjust it free and give a new date. If it is a new request outside the agreed style, explain the cost of the change politely.
Record what happened and what you changed, so you learn from it.

blocks.title: Worked example: a December rush plan
blocks.context: For example, Ronke in Lagos usually receives far more orders in December than she can finish. Last year several outfits were late and two clients left.
steps: She counts her capacity: with one trained helper, about 7 gowns a week, so about 21 gowns in the three weeks before Christmas.
She announces on WhatsApp status in October that December bookings close when 21 slots are filled, or on 30 November, whichever comes first.
Each slot needs a deposit to be confirmed; she does not 'hold' slots for promises.
She schedules fittings at least four days before each due date.
She closes bookings at 20 slots, keeping one slot free for an adjustment or emergency.
blocks.result: Ronke delivers all December orders on time, with fittings done. She turns away some work, but repeat clients return in January because they trust her dates.

blocks.title: Keep one spare slot
blocks.text: Always leave a little unbooked time in each week. Power cuts, illness and machine breakdowns happen, and spare time stops one problem from making every order late.
Write your alteration policy

A clear alteration policy protects both sides. For example: one free adjustment within 7 days of collection if the fit does not match the agreed measurements; changes to style after cutting are charged; garments altered elsewhere are not covered. Send it with your order terms, so there are no surprises.

takeaways: Quality means it fits, it is well finished and it is on time
Most fit problems come from measuring errors or skipping the fitting
Run the same pre-delivery checklist on every garment
Cap festive bookings at your real capacity and confirm slots only with deposits
A written alteration policy prevents arguments

activity.title: Run a quality audit on three garments
steps: Write the six-point pre-delivery checklist on a card and keep it by your machine.
Check the next three garments you finish against it before delivery.
Note any fault you found and fixed, and its cause.
Write your alteration policy in three or four sentences.
activity.evidence: The checklist card with three ticked garments, photos of the finished pieces and your written alteration policy.

lessons.title: Managing apprentices and helpers fairly and safely
objectives: Write a simple apprenticeship agreement that sets out training, time, fees and duties
Plan a step-by-step training path from basic tasks to full garments
Apply fair treatment, safety and child-protection principles in the workshop
Decide when to pay a helper per piece or a fixed wage

blocks.text: Apprenticeship is how many Nigerian tailors learned the trade, and how many shops grow. A good apprentice can take simple work off your hands within months. A badly managed arrangement brings wasted fabric, disputes with families and a bad name in the community. This lesson shows how to run it professionally and fairly.

blocks.name: teaching
blocks.alt: A woman teaching a learner beside a board
blocks.caption: A planned training path turns an apprentice into real help, faster and with less wasted fabric.

blocks.text: Put the agreement in writing

In many places, apprenticeship terms are agreed by word of mouth, and that is where disputes start. Write a one-page agreement, read it aloud with the apprentice and a parent or guardian where relevant, and let each side keep a copy. It should cover:

items: **Duration:** how long the training lasts and what she should be able to do at the end.
**Fees:** any training fee, how and when it is paid, and whether it includes tools.
**Hours:** working days and times, and breaks.
**Stipend or pay:** whether she earns anything, for example once she can sew garments for clients.
**Tools and materials:** what she must bring and what the shop provides.
**Conduct and safety rules:** punctuality, care of clients' fabric, phone use, safety.
**Completion:** how her skills will be assessed and how the end of training (often called 'freedom') will be marked.

blocks.text: A training path that builds skill

blocks.title: A sample training path
items: Tools, safety, threading
Straight seams on offcuts
Measuring and simple skirts
Blouses, trousers, linings
Full gown with supervision
Independent client work
blocks.caption: Each stage is signed off before the next, so client fabric is only trusted to proven skills.

blocks.text: Start on offcuts, not client fabric. Give one clear task per stage and check it. Keep a simple skills record for each apprentice with the date each skill was signed off. This record protects you if a family asks why she is not yet sewing for clients, and it gives her a sense of progress.
Fair treatment and safety

items: Speak to apprentices with respect. Correct mistakes privately and show the right way. Beating, insults and threats are abuse and have no place in a professional workshop.
Teach safety on day one: needles, scissors, the iron, electrical sockets and keeping the generator outside.
Do not keep a school-age child away from school to work in the shop. Check that young people are of working age, involve parents or guardians, and follow your state's child-protection laws.
Do not hold an apprentice's documents or wages as a threat.
Provide water, toilet access and reasonable working hours.

blocks.title: Close supervision on machines and irons
blocks.text: New learners should use the iron and electric machines only under supervision until they show they can work safely. Show where the main switch and fire extinguisher are, and what to do if a socket sparks: switch off at the main and do not touch the appliance.
Handling problems with an apprentice

When problems come up, such as lateness, careless work or damaged fabric, deal with them early and calmly. Talk privately, describe the problem with a specific example, and agree what must change and by when. Write a short note of the conversation in her record. If the problem continues, involve her parent or guardian, or the person who introduced her, before it grows into a dispute. Ending an arrangement should follow what the written agreement says.
Paying helpers: per piece or fixed wage

Once a trained helper sews for clients, you can pay a **fixed wage** (weekly or monthly) or **per piece** (a set amount for each finished garment). Per-piece pay rewards speed and suits busy seasons, but you must check quality closely. A fixed wage suits steady work and encourages care, but you must keep enough orders flowing to cover it. Whichever you choose, include the cost in your labour rate when you price.

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing per-piece pay
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Enugu has a trained helper, Uche, during the December rush. Grace prices a simple gown with 8,000 naira of labour (8 hours at 1,000 naira). All figures are approximate.
steps: Uche can sew the main construction of the gown in about 5 hours; Grace does cutting, fitting and finishing.
Grace offers Uche 5,000 naira per gown sewn to standard, matching 5 of the 8 labour hours.
Uche sews 10 gowns in two weeks and earns 50,000 naira.
Grace checks every gown against the pre-delivery checklist; 1 needs rework, which Uche fixes before payment.
Grace's own share of labour (3 hours per gown) and the overheads stay in her price, so her margin is protected.
blocks.result: Per-piece pay matched to the labour already in the price lets Grace take more orders without cutting her profit, while quality checks keep standards up.

blocks.title: Respect clients' privacy too
blocks.text: Teach apprentices that client measurements, phone numbers and photos stay in the shop. They should not post clients' outfits or contact clients privately without your permission.

takeaways: A written one-page agreement prevents most apprenticeship disputes
Train in stages on offcuts before trusting client fabric
Respect, safety and child protection are non-negotiable
Match per-piece pay to the labour cost already in your price

activity.title: Draft your apprenticeship pack
steps: Write a one-page apprenticeship agreement using the seven headings in this lesson.
Write a training path of five or six stages for your shop.
Create a skills record page with a sign-off date for each stage.
List your workshop safety rules to show on day one.
activity.evidence: Your draft agreement, training path, skills record template and safety rules (photo or document).

lessons.title: Measuring business performance and writing a monthly report
objectives: Calculate five key numbers: sales, profit, on-time delivery rate, repeat client rate and average order value
Compare one month with another to see what is improving
Write a one-page monthly report another person can understand
Choose one action for next month based on the numbers

blocks.text: A busy shop can still be losing ground. Numbers tell you what your eyes cannot: whether profit is rising, whether you keep promises, and whether clients come back. You do not need many numbers. Five, taken from your order book and cash book each month, are enough to guide good decisions.

blocks.name: data-reports
blocks.alt: A person reviewing charts and reports
blocks.caption: A short monthly report built from your own records shows where the business is going.

blocks.text: Five numbers to track

head: Number
How to calculate
What it tells you
rows: Total money received from clients in the month
Sales minus all business costs (materials, helpers, overheads)
Orders ready on or before the due date / total orders due, x 100
Orders from returning clients / total orders, x 100
Whether clients trust you enough to return
Whether you are selling higher-value work

blocks.title: Worked example: comparing April and May
blocks.context: For example, Aisha in Kano runs a small shop with one helper. She takes figures from her order book and cash book. Naira amounts are approximate.
steps: April: 20 orders due, 14 on time, so on-time rate = 14 / 20 x 100 = 70%. Repeat clients: 6 of 20 orders = 30%. Sales 400,000 naira, costs 300,000, profit 100,000 naira. Average order value = 400,000 / 20 = 20,000 naira.
In May she capped weekly bookings and added fittings four days before due dates.
May: 18 orders due, 17 on time, so 17 / 18 x 100 = about 94%. Repeat clients: 8 of 18 = about 44%.
May sales 420,000 naira, costs 290,000, profit 130,000 naira. Average order value = 420,000 / 18 = about 23,300 naira.
She took fewer orders but earned more profit and kept more promises.
blocks.result: The numbers show Aisha's capacity cap worked: on-time delivery rose from 70% to about 94%, repeat clients rose, and profit grew by about 30,000 naira, even with fewer orders.

blocks.title: The monthly review cycle
items: Record daily
Total monthly
Compare months
Choose one action
Check next month
blocks.caption: Small, regular reviews with one action at a time lead to steady improvement.

blocks.text: Writing a one-page report
A report helps you think clearly, and it is useful if you apply for a loan or grant, join a cooperative, or explain the business to a partner. Keep it to one page with these parts:

items: **Headline:** one sentence on the month, for example 'More profit from fewer, better-planned orders.'
**Numbers:** the five key numbers for this month and last month side by side.
**What went well:** two or three points with evidence (a client review, an on-time rush).
**What went wrong:** honest points, such as a late order and why it happened.
**Action for next month:** one specific change and how you will measure it.

blocks.title: One action at a time
blocks.text: If you change everything at once, you cannot tell what worked. Pick the single change most likely to help, such as raising the price of one style or adding a fitting step, and see its effect in next month's numbers.
Reading what the numbers say

items: **Sales up, profit flat:** costs rose or prices are too low. Recheck your costing, especially fabric prices and overheads.
**On-time rate falling:** you are booking beyond capacity, or losing time to rework. Cap bookings and review your quality checklist.
**Repeat rate low:** clients are not coming back. Ask why: fit, finish, delays or price.
**Average order value rising:** you are selling higher-value work, such as lined or more detailed styles, or group orders. Good, as long as the on-time rate holds.
**Big balances owed:** profit on paper but no cash. Chase collections before taking new orders.

blocks.text: Keep the five numbers in a simple table, one column per month, at the back of your order book or in a spreadsheet. After three months you will see patterns that one busy week could never show you, such as which months are slow and when to run a promotion.
Collecting client feedback

Numbers show what happened; feedback explains why. A few days after collection, send a short WhatsApp message asking two questions: 'How was the fit?' and 'What could we do better?' Note the answers in a feedback list. With permission, save positive comments to use as reviews on your page. Treat complaints as free advice: if three clients mention slow replies, that is your next action.

items: Use the same five numbers every month so comparisons are fair.
Keep each month's report in one folder, on paper or on the phone.
Look back every three months to see the trend, not just one month's change.

takeaways: Track sales, profit, on-time rate, repeat rate and average order value monthly
Compare this month with last month using the same calculations
A one-page report: headline, numbers, went well, went wrong, one action
Change one thing at a time and measure its effect
Ask every client two short feedback questions

activity.title: Write your first monthly report
steps: Use your order book and cash book for the last full month.
Calculate the five key numbers.
Send the two feedback questions to at least five recent clients.
Write your one-page report with a headline and one action for next month.
activity.evidence: Your one-page monthly report and screenshots of at least three client feedback replies.

quiz.q: A client's new cotton Ankara gown shrank after its first wash. What prevention step was most likely missed?
options: Pre-washing the cotton fabric before cutting
quiz.explain: Untreated cotton can shrink on first washing. Pre-washing before cutting, with the client's agreement, prevents this.

quiz.q: Ronke can finish about 7 gowns a week. December has three working weeks before Christmas. What is the wisest booking limit?
options: Unlimited, she will hire on the day
About 20 gowns, keeping a spare slot
quiz.explain: Capacity is about 21 gowns; booking around 20 leaves a margin for breakdowns, power cuts or adjustments.

quiz.q: An apprentice's family asks why she is not yet sewing for clients after three months. What best supports the owner's answer?
options: Asking the family to pay more
Letting her sew client fabric immediately
A skills record showing which stages are signed off and what is next
quiz.explain: A dated skills record shows progress fairly and explains why client work comes at a later stage.

quiz.q: Grace prices 8,000 naira of labour into a gown. Her helper sews about 5 of the 8 hours. Which per-piece rate keeps Grace's margin safe?
quiz.explain: At 1,000 naira per hour, 5 hours equals 5,000 naira. Paying more than the labour in the price eats into profit.

quiz.q: In June, 25 orders were due and 20 were delivered on time. What is the on-time delivery rate?
Aisha's sales were 360,000 naira from 18 orders. What is her average order value?
quiz.explain: 360,000 / 18 = 20,000 naira per order.

modules.title: Portfolio, Selling and Growth
modules.overview: Turn your finished work into a portfolio and WhatsApp Business catalogue that sells, talk about price and value with confidence, take payments safely, and finish with a certification project and a 90-day growth plan.

lessons.title: Building your portfolio and WhatsApp Business catalogue
objectives: Photograph garments clearly with a phone in natural light
Set up a WhatsApp Business profile, catalogue and collections
Write captions and catalogue entries that answer buyers' questions
Get consent before posting clients and protect their privacy

blocks.text: Most fashion clients in Nigeria now decide whether to contact a tailor after seeing her work on WhatsApp status, a WhatsApp Business catalogue or Instagram. Your portfolio is your shop window. It does not need a professional photographer. It needs clear, honest photos of your real work, organised so a client can find what she wants quickly.

blocks.name: fashion-photoshoot
blocks.alt: A person photographing a model wearing an outfit
blocks.caption: Clear photos of real garments, taken with a phone in good light, are the heart of your portfolio.

blocks.text: Taking good photos with a phone

items: **Light:** shoot in daylight near a window or outside in shade. Avoid harsh midday sun and the yellow light of indoor bulbs.
**Background:** a plain wall, curtain or sheet so the outfit stands out.
**Shots:** full front, back, side, and close-ups of details such as neckline, sleeve, embroidery and inside finishing.
**On a person or a form:** clothes look best worn. If you use a client, get her permission first.
**Clean lens and steady hands:** wipe the camera lens, hold the phone at chest height and tap the screen to focus.
**Honest edits:** crop and brighten if needed, but do not change colours or shape; the client must receive what she saw.

blocks.text: Setting up WhatsApp Business

**WhatsApp Business** is a free app from WhatsApp for small businesses. It lets you create a business profile with your address, hours and description, and a **catalogue** where each item has photos, a name, a price and a description. You can group items into **collections**, such as 'Office wear', 'Owambe styles' or 'Kids'. It also has **quick replies** for messages you send often, **labels** to sort chats (New order, Deposit paid, Ready), and greeting and away messages.

items: Install WhatsApp Business and register your business number (preferably a separate line from your personal number).
Complete the profile: business name, category, your one-sentence business statement, address or area, hours and Instagram link.
Add your best 10 to 20 garments to the catalogue, each with clear photos and a short description.
Group items into two to four collections that match your customer groups.
Create quick replies for your price guide, order terms and deposit details.
Create labels for each stage of your order workflow and use them every day.

blocks.text: Writing a catalogue entry that sells

Clients often ask the same questions: How much? How long? Can you make it in my size or fabric? Answer them in the entry so the chat starts closer to an order. Include the style name, what is included (lined or not, fabric supplied or not), a price or 'from' price, turnaround time and how to order.

blocks.title: Worked example: one catalogue entry
blocks.context: For example, Kemi in Abeokuta sews corporate wear for working women and is adding her best-selling skirt suit to her catalogue.
steps: Photos: front and back on a client (with written WhatsApp permission), plus close-ups of the collar and the lined, overlocked inside.
Name: 'Fitted peplum skirt suit (lined)'.
Price: 'From 25,000 naira sewing fee with your fabric; full package from 48,000 naira' (approximate, from her costing sheet).
Description: 'Made to your measurements. Fully lined. Ready in 10 days after deposit and fitting. One free adjustment within 7 days.'
Ordering: 'Tap Message business to book a measurement appointment.'
blocks.result: Kemi's entry answers price, turnaround and quality questions before the client types, so her chats move faster from enquiry to deposit.

blocks.title: From finished garment to post
items: Get client consent
Photograph in daylight
Light, honest edit
Write clear caption
Post to catalogue and status
Reply quickly
blocks.caption: Every finished garment can become content that brings the next order.

blocks.text: Keep the catalogue working

A catalogue is not a one-time job. Update prices whenever your costing sheet changes, remove styles you no longer make, and add new pieces as you finish them. Put your strongest, most typical work first: if most of your income is office wear, do not lead with a bridal gown you made once. When a client asks about a style, send the catalogue item itself instead of retyping details. Use your status to show work in progress, such as cutting, a fitting or pressing, because it shows that you are busy and trusted, and it reminds your contacts that you are available for orders.
Using Instagram alongside WhatsApp

Instagram works well for fashion because it is visual. Switch to a **professional account** to see insights such as reach and which posts get the most saves. Use your business statement in the bio and a link that opens your WhatsApp. Post finished pieces, short videos of a fitting or a before-and-after, and save your best styles in **Highlights** by category. Keep posting regularly rather than in bursts.

blocks.title: Consent and privacy
blocks.text: Always ask before posting a client wearing your work, and respect a 'no'. Never post a client's measurements, phone number, home address or private chats. Blur faces of children unless a parent has agreed in writing.

takeaways: Daylight, plain backgrounds and front, back and detail shots make a strong portfolio
WhatsApp Business offers a profile, catalogue, collections, quick replies and labels
Good catalogue entries answer price, turnaround and inclusions upfront
Get client consent before posting, and never share private details

lessons.title: Communicating value, handling price talk and taking payments safely
objectives: Explain the value of your work in terms clients care about
Respond to requests for discounts without losing your margin
Write a clear proposal for a group or uniform order
Take payments safely and avoid common payment scams

blocks.text: Clients rarely pay for stitches. They pay for how the outfit makes them look and feel at the event, for confidence that it will be ready on time, and for not having to worry. When you talk about your work in those terms, price becomes one part of the decision instead of the only part.

blocks.name: business-chat
blocks.alt: Two people chatting about a business deal on their phones
blocks.caption: Most fashion sales happen in chat, so clear and confident messages matter as much as good sewing.

blocks.text: Talk about value, not just price

blocks.title: Price talk vs value talk
items: Price talk
Value talk
blocks.caption: Value talk gives the client reasons to choose you that a cheaper tailor cannot copy.

items: **Fit:** 'Made to your measurements, with a fitting before finishing.'
**Finish:** 'Fully lined, every seam overlocked, so it lasts and feels good on the skin.'
**Reliability:** show your on-time record or reviews from past clients.
**Aftercare:** 'One free adjustment within 7 days.'
**Proof:** photos of similar finished work, inside and out.

blocks.text: When a client says 'Please reduce it'

Bargaining is normal in Nigerian markets, so expect it and prepare. Never drop below your total cost. Instead, keep your price and add value, or keep your margin and reduce the cost of the order. Examples: 'I can do it at 35,000 without the lining' or 'For 40,000 you also get a matching headwrap.' For loyal clients, a small, planned discount (for example on a second outfit in the same order) can be fine if your costing still shows a profit.

blocks.title: Worked example: a church choir uniform proposal
blocks.context: For example, Blessing in Benin City is asked to quote for 30 choir gowns. Her costing sheet shows about 14,000 naira total cost per gown when the church supplies fabric. All figures are approximate.
steps: She prices at a 20% margin for a bulk order: 14,000 / 0.8 = 17,500 naira per gown, total 525,000 naira.
She checks capacity: with one helper she can finish about 10 identical gowns a week, so she quotes 3 weeks from full measurements and deposit.
She asks for a 50% deposit (262,500 naira), the balance on delivery, and measurements of all 30 singers by a fixed date.
Her one-page proposal lists style, inclusions, price, deposit, timeline, fitting plan and alteration policy, with photos of similar work.
She sends it as a PDF on WhatsApp and follows up in three days.
blocks.result: The committee sees a clear, professional offer with dates they can plan around. Blessing's margin is protected even with the bulk price, because it starts from her real cost.

blocks.text: For uniform contracts with schools or companies, expect to be asked for your CAC certificate, a business account in the registered name and sometimes samples. Agree payment stages in writing before you buy anything, because some organisations pay only after delivery and you must not fund a large order from your own pocket without a deposit.
Taking payments safely

Common ways to receive payment include bank transfer to your business account, POS terminals from providers such as Moniepoint or OPay, and payment links from services such as Paystack, which let clients pay by card or transfer through a secure page. Whatever you use, the money must show in your account before a garment is released.

blocks.title: Payment scams to watch for
blocks.text: Fake credit alerts and edited screenshots: confirm in your banking app. 'Overpayment' tricks, where someone sends too much and asks for a refund, then the original payment is reversed: wait until it clears and refund only to the same account. Never share your PIN, password or OTP, and no real bank or payment company will ask for them by phone or chat.

items: Display your business account name clearly so clients can check it before sending money.
Confirm every payment in your app before releasing work.
Send a receipt showing amount paid and balance.
Record it in your cash book the same day.

blocks.text: A clear, friendly first reply

Speed and tone in the first reply win many orders. Answer enquiries within a few hours during working days, greet the client by name, and give a direct answer before asking questions. For example: 'Good afternoon, Nkem. Thank you for your message. This style is from 22,000 naira with your fabric, ready in 10 days after measurement and deposit. When would you like to come for measurement?' Save versions of this as quick replies. If you cannot reply quickly, set an away message that says when you will respond.
Reviews and referrals

Happy clients are your best marketing. After a good fitting, ask: 'Would you mind sending a short review I can share?' With permission, post it with a photo of the outfit. Ask satisfied clients to share your catalogue with friends who have events coming up. Some tailors offer a small thank-you, such as free alterations on the next order, when a referral becomes a paying client.

takeaways: Clients pay for fit, finish, reliability and peace of mind, so talk about those
Answer discount requests by changing the order, not your margin
A one-page proposal with price, deposit, timeline and terms wins group orders
Release garments only after the money shows in your account
Ask happy clients for reviews and referrals

lessons.title: Certification project and your 90-day growth plan
objectives: Assemble the evidence pack for the course capstone
Check your work honestly against the certification checklist
Write a 90-day plan with clear, measurable targets
Choose the next growth step that fits your stage

blocks.text: You have now built the core systems of a professional fashion business: a clear customer, costing and pricing, an order workflow, a cash book, quality checks, fair management of helpers, monthly measurement and a sales toolkit. This last lesson pulls them together into one evidence pack and a plan for the next three months.

blocks.name: certificate
blocks.alt: A person holding up a certificate
blocks.caption: Your certificate is earned with real evidence from your own business, not just quiz answers.

blocks.text: Your capstone evidence pack

head: Item
Comes from
Format
rows: Costing sheet for one style (full package and sewing fee)
Order book with at least five complete orders
Two weeks of cash book records and monthly profit
Quality checklist used on three garments

blocks.text: Check yourself honestly

Before you submit, go through each item and ask: is this from my real business, and is it complete? A costing sheet with guessed numbers is weaker than one built from real receipts and timed work. If something is missing, finish it before the final quiz. The point is not to impress an assessor; it is to leave the course with systems you will actually use.
Write a short reflection

In half a page, answer three questions: What did I change in my business during this course? What happened as a result, with at least one number (for example, new price, on-time rate or monthly profit)? What feedback did I receive from clients or helpers, and what did I change because of it?

Ask one person who knows your work, such as a regular client, a fellow tailor or your helper, to look at your pack and tell you one thing that is strong and one thing to improve. Note their comment and what you did about it. This short feedback step is part of the evidence standard for the course.
Your 90-day plan

blocks.title: A 90-day growth plan
items: Days 1-30: fix pricing
Days 31-60: build sales
Days 61-90: grow capacity
Day 90: review numbers
blocks.caption: Each month has one main focus and a number to check at the end.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 90-day plan
blocks.context: For example, Ada in Onitsha finishes the course with a costing sheet showing two of her popular styles were underpriced, an on-time rate of about 75%, and a new WhatsApp catalogue.
steps: Days 1 to 30: apply new prices to the two underpriced styles, announce them with a date, and track how many orders she still receives. Target: average order value up from about 20,000 to 23,000 naira.
Days 31 to 60: post two finished garments a week on WhatsApp status and Instagram, add five new catalogue items and ask every client for a review. Target: at least 6 new enquiries a week.
Days 61 to 90: train her apprentice to finish hems and press, freeing about 5 hours a week of her own time. Target: on-time rate above 90%.
Day 90: write a monthly report comparing the third month with the month before the course started.
blocks.result: Ada's plan has one focus per month, a clear target for each, and a review date, so she can see exactly what worked.

blocks.text: Making the plan stick

Write your plan on one page and put it where you see it every day, such as the wall above your machine. Break each month's focus into weekly tasks, and tick them off on Saturdays. At the end of each month, check the target number using your order book and cash book. If you missed it, ask why, adjust the next month, and keep going. A plan you review often is worth more than a perfect plan you never look at again. Share it with someone you trust, such as a fellow tailor or a member of your cooperative, and ask them to check in with you each month.
Choosing your next growth step

items: **Still underpricing or losing track of money?** Strengthen costing and bookkeeping first; growth on weak pricing only multiplies losses.
**Fully booked and turning clients away?** Train or hire help, or raise prices, before buying more machines.
**Steady bespoke income and savings?** Test a small ready-to-wear batch of one style in three or four sizes, and sell it before making more.
**Ready for contracts?** Complete your CAC business name registration and annual return, open a business account and build a proposal template for schools, churches and companies.

blocks.title: How certification works
blocks.text: To earn the Certificate of Completion in Fashion Business Management, you must submit your capstone evidence and confirm that the practical task is complete, then score at least 70% in the final quiz.

takeaways: The capstone pack shows real systems from your own business
Check every item for honesty and completeness before submitting
A good 90-day plan has one focus per month and a number to check
Fix pricing and records before scaling up
Certification needs capstone evidence plus 70% or more in the final quiz
